title: private-deploy-networking-incident-breadcrumbs-mira-singh
content:
Summary:
- Client reported failures calling Redwood private control plane from their VPC after a maintenance window (lossy DNS, TLS handshake failures intermittently).
- Impact: control-plane API calls 30-60s timeouts or TLS errors for a subset of hosts, intermittent across AZs.
- Triage notes: appears to be networking-related (egress/DNS) rather than cert rotation (no cert expiry).

Timeline (high-level):
- 2026-02-24 23:10 UTC: customer reports timeouts after our planned router upgrade in region-us-west-2.
- 2026-02-24 23:25 UTC: initial Slack triage; assigned to me.
- 2026-02-25 01:10 UTC: reproducer session with customer — observed intermittent TLS handshake failure with X509 error sometimes.
- 2026-02-26 09:40 UTC: found diffs in VPC peering route table on customer side (some routes removed during maintenance).
- 2026-03-01 15:30 UTC: added additional logging on egress NAT to capture DNS resolution times and failed connections.

Observed symptoms and errors (raw snippets):
- curl to control plane sometimes returns 52.30.1.14:443 - TLS handshake failure:
  "curl: (35) error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure"
- Some clients see: "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" but only when routed through a proxy/transparent TLS inspect appliance.
- dig output when failing:
  "; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> api.redwood.internal
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 0, AUTHORITY: 1, ADDITIONAL: 1
;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
api.redwood.internal. 300 IN NS ns-somewhere.customer.net.
;; Query time: 5039 msec"
- tcpdump (client VPC egress) shows SYN retransmits and TCP RST from intermediate appliance when destination IP is one of our-bastion NAT cluster nodes.

Commands I ran (notes + outputs):
- Validate DNS from customer host:
  dig +trace api.redwood.internal
  -> eventually falls back to customer-managed NS and times out (~5s).

- Check VPC peering routes (aws cli):
  aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=customer-peering-rt
  -> route to 10.10.0.0/16 via pcx-0abcde present in rt-a but missing in rt-b (one AZ).

- Verify TLS from our control-plane egress (from a debug pod in private deploy cluster):
  curl -v --resolve api.redwood.internal:443:52.30.1.14 https://api.redwood.internal/healthz --connect-timeout 10
  *   Trying 52.30.1.14:443...
  * Connected to api.redwood.internal (52.30.1.14) port 443 (#0)
  * TLS 1.2 connection using ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
  * server certificate: CN=api.redwood.internal
  * SSL certificate verify ok
  > GET /healthz HTTP/1.1
  < HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  (succeeds from our control plane reliably)

- From customer host via nat instance:
  curl -v https://api.redwood.internal/healthz
  * Connected to api.redwood.internal (52.30.1.14) port 443 (#0)
  * TLS handshake error (sometimes) - see error above

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Split-brain DNS/peering: customer has mixed route tables across AZs; some hosts resolve to our internal IPs but traffic is routed through an appliance that does TLS inspection causing x509 mismatch or handshake abort. Explains why some AZs are fine and others fail.
2) MTU/path MTU issues causing TLS handshake/fragmentation failures on some paths (e.g., SYN/FIN visible, then RST).
3) Transient NAT gateway misconfiguration that rewrites SNI or source IP causing our TLS policy to reject connections for a subset of IPs.
4) Mis-provisioned VPC peering acceptance state with stale route propagation so only some subnets have valid routes.

Investigation steps and findings:
- Route table audit: found missing peering route in rt-b (AZ b). Customer maintenance script pruned routes for "unused" peers and missed adding this back.
- DNS TTL and NS behavior: customer's authoritative NS returns different answers under high load; dig +trace shows referrals to an internal NS in failing AZ. Suspect their internal NS cluster has flaky health.
- Packet captures: tcpdump captured RSTs coming from an intermediate TLS inspection appliance (ip 10.254.0.45) when our IP used; captured MSS clamping difference suggesting PMTU is different through that appliance.
- Egress appliance logs (customer-provided): shows TLS handshake aborted due to "unexpected_client_hello" for a subset of sessions where client offers TLS1.3+GREASE extensions.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Asked customer to update peering route tables to include missing route (done 2026-02-26 03:10 UTC) — reduced error surface by ~60%
- Recommended bypassing TLS inspection for api.redwood.internal via their proxy/DLP policy (they created explicit bypass rule for our FQDN on 2026-02-27).
- Lowered enablement of TLS 1.3 GREASE in our client simulators for a short period to test compatibility (rolled back after tests).

Root cause (working theory):
- Combination of 1) customer-side route table missing a peering route in one AZ causing traffic to egress through a different path that 2) passes through a TLS-inspecting appliance with PMTU/MSS quirks and TLS extension incompatibility. The inspection appliance sometimes responds with RST or performs active TLS modification causing x509 errors. Also flaky authoritative NS in that AZ led to higher DNS query latency and some clients timing out and retrying over the bad path.

Open action items / next steps: (prioritized)
- (owner: customer network) Ensure all AZs have consistent peering routes and add automation guard rails to prevent the maintenance script from removing required peering routes (JIRA PD-4231).
- (owner: eng-private-deployments) Add a runbook check that validates peering route propagation for new peering attachments and alerts if any AZ lacks route (create ticket PD-4278).
- (owner: eng-sre) Add telemetry to detect "sudden TLS handshake RST from intermediate" with tagging to correlate destination IPs to peering status.
- (owner: support) Share semi-polished incident note with customer including mitigation steps and recommended proxy bypass config.
- (owner: product) Evaluate whether we should expose a control-plane health endpoint on an alternate IP/CNAME to help customers create bypass rules more easily.

Notes to self / debugging breadcrumbs for follow-up:
- If this recurs, capture full tcpdump with -s 0 on the failing host, and capture both client->appliance and appliance->destination to compare MSS and TLS ClientHello bytes.
- Add ephemeral debug pod to private deploys that can fuzz TLS ClientHello to test appliance compatibility.
- Check whether the appliance performs TLS termination (MITM) by comparing server cert chain seen by client vs. seen by our logs.
- Correlate timestamps of DNS authority flaps with route changes in customer's infra (they run automated maintenance overnight).

References and links:
- JIRA PD-4231 (customer peering route removed by maintenance)
- Confluence runbook: confluence:private-deploy-networking-runbook
- Debug scripts: github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy-scripts/pull/88

Quick reproducible steps (for SRE playbook):
1) From a host in failing AZ, run: dig +trace api.redwood.internal; note query time and authoritative NS answer.
2) Run: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 52.30.1.14 and reproduce curl for TLS handshake; capture to /tmp/trace.pcap.
3) From our side, run curl --resolve to confirm control-plane healthy.
4) If RSTs seen, ask customer to show proxy appliance logs for matching timestamps and inspect for TLS inspection rules that match api.redwood.internal.

Status: mitigations applied, error rate reduced. Waiting on customer automation fix and internal runbook ticket creation.

Personal TODO (short):
- Create PD-4278 ticket and draft runbook steps (by 2026-03-05).
- Write up a concise customer-facing summary for support to send (by 2026-03-03).

End of notes.
